etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English weghen, weȝen, from Old English wegan, from Proto-West Germanic *wegan, from Proto-Germanic *weganą (“to move, carry, weigh”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰeti, from *weǵʰ- (“to bring, transport”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To determine the weight of an object.
(transitive) Often with "out", to measure a certain amount of something by its weight, e.g. for sale.
(transitive, figuratively) To determine the intrinsic value or merit of an object, to evaluate.

quote.citation: 2011, Roy F. Baumeister, John Tierney, Willpower, →ISBN, page 103:
quote.text: As they started picking features, customers would carefully weigh the choices, but as decision fatigue set in they'd start settling for whatever the default option was.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figuratively, obsolete) To judge; to estimate.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto VII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], part II (books IV–VI), London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC, page 444:
quote.text: But ſhe thereof grew proud and inſolent, / That none ſhe worthie thought to be her fere, / But ſcornd them all, that loue vnto her ment; / Yet was ſhe lou’d of many a worthy pere, / Vnworthy ſhe to be belou’d ſo dere, / That could not weigh of worthineſſe aright.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To consider a subject. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
(intransitive, copulative, stative) To have a certain weight.
(intransitive) To have weight; to be heavy; to press down.

quote.text: If they ſhall faile, I with mine EnemiesWill triumph o're my perſon, which I waigh not,Being of thoſe Vertues vacant.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be considered as important; to have weight in the intellectual balance.

quote.text: Your vowes to her, and me, […] / Will euen weigh, and both as light as tales.

quote.citation: a. 1705, John Locke, “Of the Conduct of the Understanding”, in Posthumous Works of Mr. John Locke: […], London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], published 1706, →OCLC, § 19, page 62:
quote.text: I anſwer, this is a good Objection, and ought to weigh with thoſe whoſe Reading is deſign’d for much Talk and little Knowledge, and I have nothing to ſay to it.

definitions.definition: (transitive, nautical) To raise an anchor free of the seabed.

quote.citation: 1624, Walter Russell, Anas Todkill, Thomas Momford, “The Accidents that hapned in the Discovery of the Bay of Chisapeack”, in Iohn Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia, New-England, and the Summer Isles: […], London:  […]  I[ohn] D[awson] and I[ohn] H[aviland] for Michael Sparkes, →OCLC, book 3; reprinted in The Generall Historie of Virginia, [...] (Bibliotheca Americana), Cleveland, Oh.: The World Publishing Company, 1966, →OCLC, page 56:
quote.text: Towards the euening we wayed, & approaching the ſhoare [...], we landed where there lay a many of baskets and much bloud, but ſaw not a Salvage.

quote.text: Here we used to remain until nearly time for slack-water again, when we weighed and made for home.
